newsitem.title: MONACO: ATHLETICS-IDENTITY CARDS INTRODUCED IN DOPING FIGHT.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-IDENTITY CARDS INTRODUCED IN DOPING FIGHT.

text.p: Elite track and field athletes will carry identity cards from next year verifying that they have submitted to out-of-competition testing.
International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) president Primo Nebiolo told a news conference on Friday the top 20 athletes in each event would be issued with the card.
"Without this card and without acceptance of this programme of random, unannounced and out-of-competition testing, no athlete will be eligible for cash awards," Nebiolo said.

Asked what would happen if an athlete not ranked among the top 20 in his or her discipline went on to win a world title, Nebiolo shrugged, then replied: "We would congratulate him, then we would test him."
Nebiolo said elite performers would probably undergo three random tests a year.
"During the 1996 season we carried out 1,750 out-of-competition tests on top-level athletes," he said.
Olympic 200 and 400 metres champion Michael Johnson, one of more than 100 athletes who will attend the IAAF's annual gala dinner on Friday night, did not seem impressed with the IAAF's initiative.
"What's the big difference?," he asked. "I've been tested out of competition by the national federation and the IAAF."
Johnson and Olympic women's 800 and 1,500 metres champion Svetlana Masterkova will receive awards at the gala as "athletics legends".
Nebiolo also announced the IAAF events at which prize money will be paid for the first time from next year but refused to give any details on the total amount at stake.

Cash awards will be paid at the world outdoor and indoor championships, the World Cup, the world cross country championships, the world half marathon championships, the world road relay championships and the world race walking cup.

Nebiolo said the prize money structure would be similar to the grand prix final, the only event at present at which prize money is paid. Winners in the grand prix final get $50,000, runners-up $30,000 and third-placed athletes win $20,000.
Despite repeated questioning the IAAF chief would not reveal how much money in total was at stake.
"I don't want to be very clear," he said. "So I don't give the details."
Athletics sources told Reuters on Thursday that $10 million would be set aside for prizes.
Nebiolo's news conference followed a two-day IAAF council meeting which concluded on Wednesday night. The next council meeting in Turin in March will decide the venue of the 1999 world championships.
